profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting in an ML security research lab to organize a 6-week reproduction-and-extension study based on a published chapter about security evaluation of SVMs under evasion, poisoning, and privacy attacks. The team is preparing a workshop submission and an internal demo for the lab's secure ML initiative. The agenda is to decide what exactly will be reproduced from the chapter, how the attack pipelines will be packaged, what artifacts need to be ready for the workshop submission, and who owns each workstream. The expected outcome is a shared plan for experiments, artifact preparation, and milestone dates for a reproducible benchmark suite built around adversarial evaluation of SVMs on malware, spam, and intrusion-style datasets.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: adversarial machine learning, empirical evaluation design, academic publications
members.background: Lena leads a university-industry research group on trustworthy ML and has previously published on adversarial evaluation protocols for classical models, especially linear classifiers in security settings.
members.private_state: She wants a clean, defensible workshop paper with a polished benchmark narrative and fears the team will drift into engineering-heavy work that does not translate into publishable claims on time.
hidden_assumptions: A 'reproduction' means recreating the chapter's headline trends and qualitative conclusions, not necessarily matching every original preprocessing step or exact numeric values.
An 'artifact' for a workshop means code, configs, and a small documented run that reviewers can execute on a toy or subset setting without needing all raw security datasets.
The 'baseline attack implementation' can be a faithful modern reimplementation in current Python libraries as long as the conceptual attack procedure matches the original paper.
If they say results are 'ready by the deadline,' that means a stable draft of figures and tables must exist by the lab's internal review date two business days before submission.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: ML systems, reproducible pipelines, dataset curation, experiment infrastructure
members.background: Arjun maintains the lab's experiment stack and has worked on benchmark packaging for several security ML projects, with a strong emphasis on exact reruns and environment capture.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid another paper with brittle code and undocumented shortcuts, and is quietly trying to push the team toward a fully executable benchmark package that will remain useful after publication.
hidden_assumptions: A 'reproduction' means recreating the original pipeline as closely as possible, including data splits, feature extraction conventions, and attack parameterization, even if exact numbers still differ slightly.
An 'artifact' means a fully rerunnable package with environment locks, scripts for all tables, and access instructions for the real datasets used in the paper's main claims.

The 'baseline attack implementation' should preserve the original software behavior and preprocessing details wherever possible, including older libsvm-style conventions if those shaped the reported results.
If results are 'ready by the deadline,' that means the end-to-end pipeline has completed and generated final outputs by the official workshop submission timestamp.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'reproduce the chapter results' before extending them.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes success means reproducing the main directional findings: evasion hurts linear SVMs, poisoning degrades margins, and privacy leakage is demonstrable across representative security tasks, with approximate trends sufficient for publication.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes success means rebuilding the original experimental pipeline closely enough that the reported tables/curves can be regenerated with near-comparable settings, including original-style splits and feature preprocessing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML research meetings, 'reproduce the results' sounds standard and mutually intelligible; both are competent and supportive, so neither expects that the acceptance criterion itself differs.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They say the submission should include 'the artifact' and be 'reproducible.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a reviewer-friendly package: documented code, pinned configs, and one lightweight executable path that demonstrates the methodology, while larger or restricted datasets can be described rather than bundled end-to-end.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a complete rerun package for every headline result, with environment files, orchestration scripts, and instructions that let someone regenerate all figures using the main datasets, subject to access controls.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term 'artifact' has become overloaded in research culture; both think they are endorsing best practices, and the difference only matters later when scoping implementation effort.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They plan backwards from having figures 'ready by Thursday' and 'submission week locked.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes the real operational deadline is the lab's internal review cutoff on Thursday 5 PM local time, because anything later is unusable for PI sign-off and coauthor comments.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes the relevant deadline is the workshop portal deadline on Sunday 11:59 PM AoE, so Thursday means the pipeline should be mostly done but not necessarily frozen.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Academic teams often casually refer to the internal and external deadlines interchangeably as 'the deadline'; both use the same calendar language without noticing they anchor planning to different endpoints.

misalignment_points.topic: How to implement the baseline attack code
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'start from the baseline implementation' for evasion and poisoning.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes M2 will implement the attacks in the lab's current sklearn/JAX-compatible framework, preserving the attack logic but not the exact legacy software stack.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes he should first recreate the legacy-style setup closest to the original repository behavior, including older libsvm conventions and preprocessing quirks, and only later port it into the lab framework.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Saying 'baseline implementation' feels like a concrete procedural agreement, but both silently map it to the implementation style they personally regard as obviously correct for a security evaluation project.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this scoped to something we can turn into a clean workshop paper in six weeks. The fastest credible path is to reproduce the chapter results in the sense of recovering the main qualitative story across evasion, poisoning, and privacy, then add one tidy extension on adversary-aware design choices. I do not need us burning cycles chasing every preprocessing quirk if the headline trends are there and the benchmark framing is strong.

My preference is that we first reproduce the chapter results before we add the adversary-aware design comparisons, so the paper has a solid anchor before we branch out.

Otherwise we'll end up with another approximate story and no durable benchmark. I'll start from malware, spam, and intrusion because those give us the chapter's coverage and force us to settle splits, features, and attack settings properly.
